title: Northlake POC check-in - tiered batching canary results / mixed workload overrides
summary: Redwood shared early results from enabling workload-aware batching tier defaults on a small canary slice of Northlake’s hosted API traffic. Results showed meaningful cost/throughput gains on non-streaming summarization jobs using the cost-efficient tier, while the fast tier protected streaming first-token latency but showed a p99 regression during mixed prompt-length bursts. Northlake described a mixed workload (interactive streaming chat + background summarization + occasional long-context retrieval-augmented answers) and asked for clearer override mechanics per route and per environment. The group agreed on next experiments: split traffic by route (streaming vs non-streaming), pin fast tier for the streaming endpoint, run standard vs cost-efficient for background jobs, and review per-tier dashboards with reason codes to validate selection logic and avoid tail latency regressions.
topics: Canary results: latency (TTFT, p95/p99) vs throughput and $/1K tokens
Mixed workload behavior: streaming + long prompts + concurrency spikes
Override needs: per-route tier selection and precedence
Reason codes and observability: why a profile was selected
Next-step experiment design and success criteria

next_steps: Redwood turns on tiered defaults for Northlake canary: 10% traffic on hosted API, with /v1/chat:stream pinned to fast tier.
Northlake runs background summarization jobs with an explicit override (standard then cost-efficient) and compares p95/p99 + cost metrics.
Joint review early next week: look at reason codes (default vs override vs overload mode) and identify any tail regressions correlated with prompt-length buckets.
If fast-tier p99 regression repeats, Redwood will trial the tighter wait budget + admission control tweak on Northlake canary only.
transcript:
Northlake POC check-in - tiered batching canary results / mixed workload overrides
Recorded: 2026-02-12 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Nikhil Sharma, Lena Fischer, Jonas Weber, Aisha Bello
- Northlake: Elena Ruiz, Samir Patel, Maya Chen, Tom Baird

Auto-generated (Fireflies)
Summary: (see above)

[00:00] Nikhil Sharma: Cool. I think we’re all on. Uh, Elena, Samir, Maya, Tom — thanks for making time. Today we wanted to share what we’re seeing from the tiered batching canary we enabled last week, and then talk about how to handle your mixed workload without you having to babysit 10 knobs.

[00:18] Elena Ruiz: Sounds good. We have a bunch of questions, especially around… like, can we force fast for the streaming endpoint, because support agents will scream if it feels slower.

[00:28] Nikhil Sharma: Yep. That’s like the number one thing we hear. Lena has the numbers. Lena, you want to walk through the canary slice?

[00:35] Lena Fischer: Yeah. So we turned on tier selection defaults for 5% of your hosted traffic in us-east-1 only. We left everything else untouched. For that canary cohort, the policy was: streaming requests default to fast, non-streaming default to standard, and then we trialed cost-efficient on the background summarization route you flagged.

[00:57] Lena Fischer: Big picture: throughput improved on the non-streaming by about 18 to 24% depending on the hour. Cost per 1K tokens, measured on our side with the metering proxy, was down around 11% for that route. Latency wise, for non-streaming, p95 got slightly better, p99 was flat.

[01:17] Samir Patel: That’s for summarization jobs?

[01:19] Lena Fischer: Correct, the batch-ish summarization. For streaming chat: time-to-first-token stayed within target. We’re basically flat at p50 and p95. But we did see a p99 bump during the 10am to 11am local window when your concurrency spikes.

[01:36] Tom Baird: How big of a bump?

[01:38] Lena Fischer: On that window, p99 TTFT went from about 480ms baseline to about 710ms for fast tier. Not like catastrophic, but it’s a regression and it’s the kind of thing that triggers your client-side retries, so we don’t want that.

[01:56] Aisha Bello: And just to add, we also saw queue depth grow in that window. It didn’t blow up, but it’s consistent with fast tier getting “stuck” behind a few long-prefill requests when the prompt-length mix changes.

[02:11] Maya Chen: That matches what we see. We have the agent chat, which is mostly short prompts, but sometimes it’s RAG and it drags in, I don’t know, 8k tokens context. So it’s the same route. That’s the mixed workload problem.

[02:25] Nikhil Sharma: Yep, exactly. The tier by itself won’t magically separate that, unless we split routes or use workload signals. Jonas, do you want to talk about what signals we’re actually using in the canary?

[02:36] Jonas Weber: Sure. Today the selection logic is pretty simple: streaming flag, prompt length bucket, and observed concurrency. So a streaming request with a long prompt can still trigger a more conservative batching behavior. But the fast tier is supposed to bias toward “don’t wait,” not “batch harder.” The p99 bump suggests we need tighter admission control when long-prefill shows up during the peak.

[03:00] Elena Ruiz: Sorry, can I ask a basic question? Like, if we don’t set anything, we get… what tier?

[03:05] Nikhil Sharma: For hosted, default is standard unless the route is marked interactive streaming, then fast. But we can override at the route policy level. That’s what we want to do for you: explicit fast on the streaming endpoint, and explicit cost-efficient on background.

[03:22] Elena Ruiz: And that override is in Console, or via API?

[03:25] Nikhil Sharma: Both. Console route policy is the cleanest for production. For testing, you can also pass a header in the SDK — we’ve been calling it “batching-tier” internally. It’ll show up in the “effective profile” view.

[03:40] Maya Chen: Okay, because our backend team can do a header in staging quickly. In prod we prefer config.

[03:47] Tom Baird: But I want to make sure it’s not like per-request random stuff that breaks caching or something.

[03:52] Lena Fischer: The tier selection doesn’t change caching semantics. It changes scheduler wait budgets and max batch tokens and some prefill/decode balancing. KV cache is still KV cache; the thing that could change is you might see different batching patterns which change the distribution of decode interleaving.

[04:14] Samir Patel: Do you have the actual knob values? Like max wait ms, max batch tokens.

[04:20] Lena Fischer: We can share the current candidate set for your model family, yes. For fast tier, max_wait is basically near-zero, like 1 to 2ms, and max batch tokens is capped. For cost-efficient, we allow higher max batch tokens and a larger wait budget, but we also have guardrails on queue size.

[04:40] Samir Patel: When you say guardrails, is that load shedding?

[04:43] Aisha Bello: It’s a mix. Under overload we can do admission control — reject early with 429/503 depending on the policy — and we can also switch to a “degraded mode” where we stop trying to form large batches and keep the queue short. For fast tier specifically, we bias toward protecting tail latency rather than squeezing throughput.

[05:07] Tom Baird: And do we get visibility into when it switches modes?

[05:10] Aisha Bello: Yes, that’s the “reason codes” piece. You’ll see labels like: tier_default, customer_override, model_constraint, overload_mode. It’s not perfect yet, but it’s already in the canary.

[05:25] Elena Ruiz: I like that. Because right now when latency spikes we just argue about whose fault it is.

[05:31] Nikhil Sharma: (laughs) Yeah. The goal is to remove the mystery.

[05:36] Nikhil Sharma: Let’s talk about your workload shape, just to make sure we’re testing the right split. Elena, you said interactive agent chat is the big one. What about the summarization jobs — are those the “ticket wrap-up” things?

[05:49] Elena Ruiz: Exactly. After the chat, we summarize the conversation and propose tags. That doesn’t need to be real time. It just needs to finish within, like, a minute.

[05:59] Nikhil Sharma: Great candidate for cost-efficient.

[06:02] Samir Patel: We also do an internal “knowledge base refresh” thing. It’s embeddings mostly, separate.

[06:08] Nikhil Sharma: Ok, embeddings are separate path, batching tiers are for generation here.

[06:13] Maya Chen: The tricky one is the RAG answers. It’s still streaming to the agent, but the prompt is huge sometimes. That’s where we saw TTFT spikes even before.

[06:24] Lena Fischer: Right. And that’s where prompt length buckets matter. We saw that your canary traffic had more “long prefill” than we expected — like 12% in the >4k bucket in that peak hour.

[06:39] Samir Patel: That sounds right. We have one customer with giant policies they paste.

[06:44] Jonas Weber: So one experiment we can do is: keep fast tier for streaming always, but add additional protections for long-prompt streaming. That could mean more aggressive admission control when queue depth is above threshold, or a separate policy: if streaming && prompt_length > X, then cap concurrency or route to standard tier behavior. That’s a product question too, because you don’t want “fast” to mean “always accept anything.”

[07:11] Elena Ruiz: Yeah, but we also don’t want to tell agents “sorry, your answer is rejected.”

[07:15] Tom Baird: We’d rather slow down than error, within reason.

[07:18] Aisha Bello: Understood. We can tune so we degrade by limiting batching rather than shedding, until you hit an absolute ceiling. But we should agree on what “absolute ceiling” looks like.

[07:31] Nikhil Sharma: For the POC, we can set conservative thresholds so you don’t see new errors. The cost of that is you might not get full cost savings during peak. That’s okay for now.

[07:42] Elena Ruiz: What do you need from us?

[07:44] Jonas Weber: Two things: (1) prompt length distribution per route, and (2) your peak concurrency window and if it’s predictable. With that we can validate the profiles and decide if we recommend splitting the route or letting the scheduler do more work.

[08:03] Samir Patel: I can pull logs. We don’t store prompts, but we can log token counts. We can give you histograms.

[08:10] Nikhil Sharma: Perfect. Token count histograms is what we want.

[08:15] Lena Fischer: Also, are you using streaming everywhere in chat?

[08:18] Maya Chen: Yes. The agent UI expects partial tokens.

[08:21] Lena Fischer: Got it.

[08:23] Nikhil Sharma: Let’s go back to the canary findings. Lena, can you break down the cost savings again, and any “gotchas” you noticed.

[08:32] Lena Fischer: Sure. For the summarization route, cost-efficient tier increased average batch size. Mean batch tokens went from ~1.3k to ~2.1k. GPU utilization was higher and more stable. The gotcha is: if you accidentally run interactive traffic under cost-efficient, TTFT will degrade. That’s why we want route-level defaults and not “one tier for everything.”

[08:55] Elena Ruiz: That’s our concern. We have devs who will copy/paste config without understanding.

[09:01] Nikhil Sharma: That’s exactly why we’re shipping it as defaults with guardrails and “why this profile” in Console. But for your POC, we’ll keep it explicit.

[09:12] Tom Baird: On the fast tier p99 bump, do you know root cause?

[09:16] Lena Fischer: Hypothesis: long-prefill requests arrived in a burst and occupied prefill slots, and because we were still trying to do some batching even in fast tier, the short requests waited behind those. We can tighten the “wait budget” and the anti-starvation logic so short streaming requests don’t get queued behind long ones.

[09:38] Aisha Bello: You can see it in the queue depth graph: depth stayed low overall, but the “oldest request age” spiked. That’s classic head-of-line blocking.

[09:49] Samir Patel: That makes sense.

[09:51] Elena Ruiz: So what are we deciding today? Like, do we keep canary on or pause it.

[09:57] Nikhil Sharma: My recommendation: keep canary on, but adjust it so your streaming route is pinned to fast tier with stricter protections, and your summarization stays in cost-efficient. We can keep total canary at 10% and watch. If we see TTFT p99 above your agreed threshold again, we roll back same day.

[10:20] Tom Baird: What’s the rollback mechanism?

[10:22] Nikhil Sharma: Feature flag at org/route policy level. We can flip it without redeploying your side.

[10:28] Maya Chen: Okay.

[10:30] Jonas Weber: And for the experiment design: I’d like you to run the summarization route as standard for 24 hours, then cost-efficient for 24 hours, same time windows, so we can compare apples-to-apples. If you can’t do that, we can do traffic split 50/50 by request ID.

[10:52] Samir Patel: We can do the 24 hour toggles in staging but prod is tricky. For prod we can maybe do a split with a header based on job type.

[11:01] Nikhil Sharma: Header-based split is fine. We’ll track effective tier in telemetry.

[11:07] Elena Ruiz: Is there any risk this impacts data logging or retention? Our security team asked.

[11:13] Nikhil Sharma: No changes to data handling. Tier selection only affects scheduling. Logs/audit are the same. Aisha, anything to add?

[11:22] Aisha Bello: Yeah, no new payload logging. We do add a tier label to metrics, but we’re controlling cardinality so it doesn’t explode.

[11:31] Tom Baird: Good.

[11:33] Maya Chen: One more thing — overrides. We had a case where an override didn’t take effect in another system (not you), because it got overwritten by a global default. What’s the precedence here?

[11:44] Lena Fischer: Precedence is: customer override > route policy > system tier default. And if a model has a hard constraint (like a quantization variant that can’t do a certain batch size), that can clamp things but it should emit a reason code like model_constraint.

[12:03] Maya Chen: Great. Can we see “effective profile” somewhere?

[12:07] Nikhil Sharma: In Console we’ll show effective tier and the key derived knobs. For now, we can share a dashboard panel that shows selected tier and reason codes.

[12:18] Elena Ruiz: That would be fine.

[12:20] (crosstalk)

[12:21] Samir Patel: Sorry — do you also do something different for streaming chunk sizes? Because we noticed chunking can feel different.

[12:28] Lena Fischer: We’re not changing chunking behavior in this project. If chunking feels different, it might be secondary effects from scheduling — like tokens arriving in slightly different cadence. But we’re not altering the streamer.

[12:42] Samir Patel: Got it.

[12:44] Nikhil Sharma: Okay, maybe we jump to the concrete plan. Here’s what I’m hearing:
- Pin fast tier for /v1/chat:stream.
- Keep standard as default for other interactive but non-streaming, if any.
- Use cost-efficient for summarization background.
- Watch TTFT p99 and queue depth during the 10-11am local peak.

[13:08] Tom Baird: And error rate. If 429s start showing up, that’s a fire drill.

[13:12] Aisha Bello: Yep. We’ll set the guardrails to avoid 429s unless you truly saturate. And we’ll alert internally first — not page you.

[13:22] Elena Ruiz: Thank you.

[13:24] Jonas Weber: And please send prompt length histograms. That will help us decide if we need a different long-prompt path.

[13:31] Samir Patel: Will do.

[13:33] Nikhil Sharma: Great. Let’s quickly review the canary dashboards so everyone knows what we’re looking at.

[13:39] Aisha Bello: I’ll describe since I can’t screen share here. We have panels for:
- TTFT p50/p95/p99 by tier
- end-to-end latency for non-streaming by tier
- queue depth and oldest request age
- batch size distribution (tokens)
- reason code counts

[14:00] Aisha Bello: The thing we care about for you is TTFT p99 in fast tier and oldest request age. If oldest request age spikes, it suggests head-of-line blocking. If reason codes show overload_mode, we’re in a degraded path.

[14:17] Tom Baird: Can we get those numbers by region? We have some EU traffic too.

[14:21] Aisha Bello: Canary is only us-east right now. Once we’re confident, we can extend to eu-west, but one region at a time.

[14:30] Elena Ruiz: That’s fine.

[14:32] Maya Chen: Also, we have a staging environment. Can we turn it on there fully?

[14:37] Nikhil Sharma: Yes, that’s easy. We can enable it 100% in staging so you can test overrides without risk.

[14:46] Lena Fischer: In staging you may not have enough load to reproduce the p99 issue. But it’s still useful for correctness and “does override work.”

[14:55] Samir Patel: True.

[14:57] Nikhil Sharma: Any other concerns?

[15:01] Elena Ruiz: Just messaging. If we tell our execs “fast tier,” they’ll assume it’s always faster. But it’s more like… optimized for low latency at the cost of throughput, right?

[15:12] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly. We try to be careful: fast is “protect tail latency,” standard is “balanced,” cost-efficient is “lower cost, higher batching, slower tails.” We’ll share the customer-facing explanation we’re drafting.

[15:28] Jonas Weber: And the key is: fast tier should not regress your p99. If it does, that’s a bug for us, not “expected tradeoff.”

[15:38] Tom Baird: Good to hear.

[15:41] (brief silence)

[15:43] Maya Chen: Quick question: if we pass the header, does it override route config?

[15:47] Lena Fischer: Yes. Header override wins. But we recommend not leaving that in production permanently unless you have a good reason, because it can drift.

[15:58] Maya Chen: Got it.

[16:00] Nikhil Sharma: Okay, let’s do recap and owners.

[16:03] Nikhil Sharma: Lena will update the canary config: fast pinned for stream route with the stricter protections.

[16:09] Lena Fischer: Yep, I can do that today. Should be in place by tomorrow morning.

[16:13] Nikhil Sharma: Aisha will send the dashboard link and what to watch.

[16:17] Aisha Bello: Yes.

[16:18] Nikhil Sharma: Jonas will send the experiment outline for standard vs cost-efficient on summarization.

[16:23] Jonas Weber: Yep.

[16:24] Nikhil Sharma: And Samir and Maya will send token count histograms and confirm routes and header testing.

[16:30] Samir Patel: Yup.

[16:31] Maya Chen: Yes.

[16:33] Elena Ruiz: Can we schedule the next review now? Maybe Tuesday same time?

[16:38] Nikhil Sharma: Tuesday works. We’ll send an invite.

[16:41] Tom Baird: One last thing — if we see issues, do we go through support or Slack?

[16:46] Nikhil Sharma: For the POC, just email me and we’ll loop in on-call. If it’s urgent, we can also spin a shared channel.

[16:54] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[16:56] Nikhil Sharma: Thanks all. Talk soon.

[17:00] Meeting ended

(Note: Transcript may contain inaccuracies due to automated transcription.)
